distinction-01 · draft

Distinction

Definition

A difference recognized or drawn between things, meanings, or possibilities.

Recognize it

Identify the feature or criterion by which two cases differ.

Examples

Separating uncertainty about the answer from ambiguity in the question.

Counterexamples

Treating two synonyms as different concepts solely because their spellings differ.

Context

The task determines which differences matter; a useful distinction in one task may be irrelevant in another.

Limits

A distinction may be graded or contested. Excluding an alternative does not fully define positive content. This entry concerns differentiation, not distinction as honor, rank, or excellence. The project aphorism “distinction is negation” is a separate philosophical proposition.

Expressions

Distinction [en]: Differentiation or recognition of difference. English-language pilot; no claim of universality or cross-language identity.

Relationships

  • supports → ambiguity-01: Helps separate alternative interpretations. (proposed)
  • supports → vagueness-01: Helps distinguish multiple readings from unclear boundaries. (proposed)

Sources

  • Collins dictionaries, Distinction. Differentiation/difference senses; excludes honor and excellence senses. https://www.collinsdictionary.com/us/dictionary/english/distinction

ambiguity-01 · draft

Ambiguity

Definition

The availability of more than one distinct meaning or reading of a linguistic expression.

Recognize it

Can you paraphrase two distinct readings of the expression? Merely lacking a detail does not by itself establish ambiguity.

Examples

“I saw her duck” can concern an animal or a movement.

Counterexamples

A single meaning with an unclear cutoff for “tall” illustrates vagueness.

Context

Context can favor one reading while leaving others possible. Deliberate ambiguity can serve artistic or social purposes.

Limits

This is the narrower linguistic sense. Different implications or uncertain intentions do not by themselves establish multiple lexical meanings. Ambiguity can coexist with vagueness and does not establish deception.

Expressions

Ambiguity [en]: Linguistic multiplicity of meaning. English-language pilot; no claim of universality or cross-language identity.

Relationships

  • contrasts-with → vagueness-01: Alternative readings differ from unclear applicability boundaries. (proposed)
  • can-produce → uncertainty-01: Multiple readings can leave someone unsure which applies. (proposed)

Sources

  • Adam Sennet, Ambiguity. Introduction; sections 2.1–2.3 and 3. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ambiguity/
  • Roy Sorensen, Vagueness. Introduction; sections 1–2. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/vagueness/

Compared with the listed sources using AI assistance; independent specialist review pending.

vagueness-01 · draft

Vagueness

Definition

A feature of an expression whose application admits borderline cases, even when the intended sense is understood.

Recognize it

Are there borderline cases even when the intended meaning is understood?

Examples

Without a stated threshold, “a short walk” has borderline cases.

Counterexamples

“Bank” meaning a financial institution or a river edge illustrates distinct readings.

“Someone submitted the form” leaves the person unspecified; lack of that detail alone does not establish a vague category boundary.

Context

Purpose, comparison class and agreed thresholds can sharpen an application without removing every borderline case.

Limits

Vagueness differs from generality and missing detail, can be useful, and can coexist with ambiguity. Philosophical accounts disagree about what explains borderline cases. A stipulated cutoff serves a purpose; it need not discover a pre-existing exact boundary.

Expressions

Vagueness [en]: Borderline applicability. English-language pilot; no claim of universality or cross-language identity.

Relationships

  • contrasts-with → ambiguity-01: A boundary can be unclear within one reading. (proposed)
  • can-produce → uncertainty-01: Borderline cases can leave someone unsure whether a label applies. (proposed)

Sources

  • Roy Sorensen, Vagueness. Introduction; sections 1–2. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/vagueness/
  • Adam Sennet, Ambiguity. Introduction; sections 2.1–2.3 and 3. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ambiguity/

uncertainty-01 · draft

Uncertainty

Definition

Limited confidence or lack of settled knowledge about a claim, interpretation, or outcome.

Recognize it

State what you are unsure about and what information could change that.

Examples

You understand a forecast but are unsure whether rain will occur.

Counterexamples

A clearly understood question with a known answer does not create uncertainty merely by being complex.

Context

Uncertainty depends on whose information and confidence are at issue, and can remain despite precise language.

Limits

A pilot working definition, not a complete technical taxonomy. Felt confidence and epistemic warrant can come apart: someone can feel certain without adequate grounds. No probability measure is assumed.

Expressions

Uncertainty [en]: A person’s unsettled confidence or epistemic position. English-language pilot; no claim of universality or cross-language identity.

Relationships

  • contrasts-with → ambiguity-01: A person can be unsure even when an expression has one clear reading. (proposed)
  • contrasts-with → vagueness-01: A precise boundary does not guarantee knowledge about a case. (proposed)

Sources

  • Baron Reed, Certainty. Section 1, psychological versus epistemic certainty. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/certainty/

context-01 · draft

Context

Definition

The surrounding circumstances relevant to interpreting an expression, event, or claim.

Recognize it

Ask who, when, where, for what purpose, and against which background.

Examples

“It is cold” can concern weather, food, or a room, depending on the conversation.

Counterexamples

An unrelated fact about the speaker does not automatically help interpret the claim.

Context

Relevant context depends on the interpretive task; selecting context itself involves judgment.

Limits

A pilot umbrella definition. Technical accounts differ over what belongs to context. Context sensitivity is not automatically ambiguity; relevant circumstances can help interpretation without fully settling it.

Expressions

Context [en]: Circumstances relevant to interpretation. English-language pilot; no claim of universality or cross-language identity.

Relationships

  • informs → distinction-01: A purpose can determine which differences are relevant. (proposed)
  • informs → ambiguity-01: Surrounding circumstances can favor one interpretation. (proposed)
  • informs → vagueness-01: A comparison class can clarify application boundaries. (proposed)
  • informs → uncertainty-01: Background evidence can alter confidence without guaranteeing certainty. (proposed)

Sources

  • Kepa Korta and John Perry, Pragmatics. Introduction, context and utterance-specific facts. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/pragmatics/

Compared with the listed sources using AI assistance; independent specialist review pending.

Worked situation

Multiple readings

I saw her duck.

What is given

Only the written sentence is supplied.

ambiguity-01

One reading concerns seeing her animal; another concerns seeing her lower her head. More surrounding language can favor one reading.

uncertainty-01

A reader may be unsure which reading was intended. That uncertainty is an effect on the reader, distinct from the expression’s multiple readings.

Reflect

Which reading fits, and what additional sentence would help?

Sources

  • Adam Sennet, Ambiguity. Introduction; sections 2.1–2.3 and 3. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ambiguity/

Worked situation

A borderline category

Take a short walk.

What is given

No duration, distance, comparison class, or purpose is supplied.

vagueness-01

Within the intended walking sense, some distances or durations can be borderline for “short.” This is different from offering two distinct word meanings.

context-01

A walking task and an agreed duration can make the request more usable. The chosen cutoff is a practical agreement, not proof of the one true meaning.

Reflect

What purpose and comparison class matter, and would an agreed duration help?

Sources

  • Roy Sorensen, Vagueness. Introduction; sections 1–2. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/vagueness/
  • Kepa Korta and John Perry, Pragmatics. Introduction, context and utterance-specific facts. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/pragmatics/

Worked situation

Two difficulties together

Meet me by the large bank.

What is given

Only this instruction is known; no location or size criterion is supplied.

ambiguity-01

“Bank” permits a financial-institution reading and a river-edge reading.

vagueness-01

Within a reading, “large” may still have borderline applications. Multiple meanings and borderline boundaries can occur together.

context-01

A prior conversation or a location can help identify the intended place. Ask rather than assuming which reading is correct.

Reflect

Which bank, and what identifiable location would make the instruction actionable?

Sources

  • Adam Sennet, Ambiguity. Introduction; sections 2.1–2.3 and 3. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ambiguity/
  • Roy Sorensen, Vagueness. Introduction; sections 1–2. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/vagueness/

Worked situation

Meaning and inference

A friend replies, “Fine.”

What is given

The word was received. Tone, preceding question, and circumstances are not given.

context-01

Agreement, reluctance, or reassurance are possible communicative interpretations. They are not established emotions or proof of multiple lexical senses.

vagueness-01

If “fine” means acceptable, the boundary of acceptable may be unclear.

uncertainty-01

You may be unsure about the friend’s intention. Ask a clarifying question rather than inferring deception.

Reflect

What did you observe, what did you infer, and what could you ask next?

Sources

  • Kepa Korta and John Perry, Pragmatics. Introduction, context and utterance-specific facts. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/pragmatics/
  • Baron Reed, Certainty. Section 1, psychological versus epistemic certainty. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/certainty/

Worked situation

A clear statement, an uncertain event

The forecast assigns a 40% chance of rain tomorrow.

What is given

The forecast expresses a probability; no ambiguity in its wording is assumed for this exercise.

uncertainty-01

Even with the statement understood, the reader does not know whether rain will occur.

distinction-01

Separate understanding what a claim says from knowing how an event will turn out.

Reflect

What is understood, and what outcome remains unsettled?

Sources

  • Baron Reed, Certainty. Section 1, psychological versus epistemic certainty. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/certainty/
